name: Jonas Klimt
summary: Jonas is a PhD student in industrial ecology working on the prospective environmental impact assessment of mineral raw material supply for the twin (‘green & digital’) transition. In 2024, Jonas completed his Industrial Ecology M.Sc. studies at Leiden Unversity and TU Delft in the Netherlands. His master thesis compared prospective environmental impacts of freight transport by road and rail. Before this, he worked as a consultant assessing GHG footprints. He also holds a Industrial Engineering B.Sc. degree from the University of Augsburg, Germany. Jonas works on the prospective Life Cycle Assessment (pLCA) of mineral raw materials crucial for the ‘green and digital’ twin transition. His work is part of the EU funded research project RAWCLIC.

name: Ingeborg Kluts
summary: Ingeborg is an environmental scientist with a passion for sustainability education. She lectures in the bachelor's and master's programmes at the Institute of Environmental Sciences (CML). Before joining CML, she taught in various sustainability programmes at Utrecht University and Wageningen University. Through her teaching, she strives to make a small but meaningful contribution to educating future impact and change makers. She especially enjoys motivating and empowering students to learn, grow, and develop the skills and competencies they need to achieve their goals. Academic background Ingeborg holds a Master's degree in Environmental Sciences from Wageningen University. Her studies and subsequent research focused on assessing and quantifying the environmental impacts of agriculture and the energy transition, as well as conducting economic analyses of energy technologies and systems.

name: Arjan de Koning
summary: Arjan de Koning graduated in 1996 in environmental hygienics from Wageningen Agricultural University. From 1996 to 2000 he worked as a researcher at the Energy Research Centre of the Netherlands (ECN). Topic of his research was the measurement and modelling of the interaction of trace amounts of radiocaesium (137Cs) with soils and sediments. Since 2000 he is employed as a researcher at the Institute of Environmental Sciences at Leiden University, department of Industrial Ecology. His research focuses mainly on environmental chemistry and Life Cycle Impact Assessment.

name: Guusje Koorneef
summary: Guusje Koorneef is a soil scientist that is fascinated by the ecological mechanisms underlying natural soil functions and connecting with social sciences to research effective interventions for sustainable agriculture Guusje Koorneef is a soil scientist whose research has been focused on soil health in a broad sense: from investigating the ecological mechanisms that determine soil health, to developing inter- and transdisciplinary roadmaps that identify how we can better develop and use soil knowledge to improve soil health. She worked during her PhD at Wageningen University in the Vital Soils for Sustainable Intensification consortium led by Netherlands Institute for Ecology (NIOO-KNAW). She investigated how the soil organic carbon cycle can be managed in relation to soil health to improve the sustainability of arable farming. Given the central role of the carbon cycle in ecological soil processes, she worked across all (biological, chemical physical) domains of soil sciences. In the postdoc in the European Soils for Europe (SOLO) consortium, she investigated what knowledge society needs to increase the European surface area of healthy soils from 40 to 100% by 2050. She synthesized nine transdisciplinary research roadmaps that outline the required knowledge to achieve the European soil health objectives, as developed by transdisciplinary think tanks. The result of this interdisciplinary synthesis was a holistic overarching research agenda, advising the European Commission on shaping future funding calls in Mission Soil. In parallel, she established a four-part workshop series with regional stakeholders to co-develop a roadmap on how to generate and disseminate knowledge required to improve soil health in agricultural lands in the Achterhoek region. The research of Guusje will continue connecting soils, ecology and people in a systems approach as basis for sustainable agriculture. Her research will therefore span multiple scientific fields, including soil sciences, ecology, agronomy, social sciences and humanities. Examples of scientific approaches range from field work, experiments and laboratory work to workshops, surveys and textual analysis.

name: Anniek Kortleve
summary: Anniek started as a PhD researcher at the Industrial Ecology department of CML in September 2021. She currently holds a postdoctoral position at the same institute. In 2019, Anniek received her BSc diploma in Future Planet Studies with a major in Earth Sciences at the University of Amsterdam. She then continued her studies with a joint degree study of Delft University of Technology and Leiden University. She pursued a joint MSc degree in Industrial Ecology in 2021. For her MSc thesis, she assessed the carbon storage potential of urban soils in a medium-sized city in the Netherlands. Anniek began her PhD in September 2021 at the Institute of Environmental Science (CML) at Leiden University. Her doctoral research focused on socio-economic and spatial extensions of input-output models, with particular emphasis on plant-rich food system transformations. Her PhD was supervised by Dr. José Mogollón, Prof.dr. Paul Behrens, and Prof.dr. Arnold Tukker. Her research integrated physical input-output models with farm-level and subnational data and developed an open-source regionalisation method (as part of the ‘Decarbonizing Denmark 70by30: Getting the data right’ project) for policy-relevant analysis of European food system transitions. In her postdoc, Anniek will continue her work on food-system transformation.

name: Philipp Kropf
summary: Philipp Kropf is a PhD researcher on Ecotoxicology at CML since November 2023. Philipp Kropf received his BSc Biology and a MSc Molecular Ecology at the University in Bayreuth in which he gained a deeper interest on computational ecology and toxicology. As his master project he developed a machine learning program that automatically analyses sub lethal effects in images of Daphnia ssp., which streamlines analysis and allows researchers to use more data. His research tries to understand the ecotoxicological impact of chemicals on biodiversity and ecosystem services. One aim is to build predictive models on ecosystem services, taking into account diversity and species loss.

name: Alp Kuvrag
summary: Alp joined CML as a PhD candidate in September 2026 within the SPROUT project to investigate viable business models of greenhouse energy hubs for large-scale implementation. Alp completed his BSc in Industrial Engineering and Management at the University of Groningen, following the Production Technology and Logistics track. He then earned his MSc in Complex Systems Engineering and Management at TU Delft, specializing in Energy Markets and Future Energy Systems. Reflecting a versatile research background, his BSc thesis focused on developing porous stainless steel (SS-316L) structures via selective laser melting (SLM) for implant applications, while his MSc thesis developed a resilience assessment framework to evaluate how operational adaptations impact healthcare quality under disruption (COVID-19). In September 2026, he joined the Institute of Environmental Sciences (CML) at Leiden University as a PhD candidate working on the SPROUT project in collaboration with TU Delft. Alp's research focuses on upscaling the models for designing and optimizing multi-carrier energy hubs to a full implementation by the greenhouse horticulture sector. The research aims to identify viable business models, evaluate synergies with neighboring hubs or regional infrastructure, and quantify technical, governance, and social barriers to turn greenhouses into system-positive energy hubs that mitigate grid congestion and support the Dutch energy transition.

name: Joran Lammers
summary: The quality of the landscape is a good indicator of the health of a society. Joran received his Msc-diploma in Landscape Architecture in 2019 at the Wageningen University. For his final thesis he developed a spatial strategy for placing and designing XXL-warehousing in the landscape of the Netherlands. In 2020, Joran started as a landscape designer and design researcher at Strootman Landschapsarchitecten. Among his projects are the design research ‘Ontspannen Nederland,' were a spatial strategy for solving the nitrogen problem was developed, and on 'Agroforestry 1+1=3,' which provides a landscape perspective on the development of agroforestry in the Dutch landscape. Joran started as a PhD researcher and teacher at CML in August 2023. Here, he continued a collaborative project of CML and Strootman Landschapsarchitecten called ‘Nederland Veganland?’, a research by design thought experiment. What if all of the Netherlands switched to a 100% plant-based diet? What would that mean for the layout of the country? For climate justice? For the economy? Next to his research activities, Joran coordinates and explores a new initiative from Leiden-Delft-Erasmus Universities. It focuses on connecting the themes of climate change and biodiversity loss into applied and interdisciplinary research and education. The white paper 'Connect Climate and Biodiversity' is the first product of this initiative. Joran conducts design research into (food) landscapes of the future. With his background in landscape architecture, he is able to visualize landscapes, from national to local scale levels. He uses this skill for the development of future scenarios where a balance is sought between the consumption needs of people on the one hand (food, energy, etc.) and the needs for our living environment on the other hand (clean air, nature quality, soil quality, water safety, etc.). "His work is driven by the beauty of the dynamic river delta of the Netherlands and the urgency to use landscape quality as the foundation for further development."

name: Kai Li
summary: Kai joined the Industrial Ecology department at CML as a PhD researcher in February 2021. His research centers on assessing and mitigating the environmental impacts of the global plastic waste trade. Kai Li graduated in 2020 with a MSc degree in Management Science and Engineering at Chongqing University after receiving his BSc degree in Construction Management at Wuhan University of Technology in 2017. During his MSc, Kai did research on Chinese farmland transactions with the knowledge of urban and land economics. In 2019, he took part in a project aiming to measure energy consumption and operational carbon emissions in the Chinese building sector, which supports his final thesis. Kai is developing a model to quantify the environmental impacts of the global plastic waste trade. His work involves reconciling bilateral trade data, evaluating recycling rates, modeling environmental consequences, and analyzing the effects of related policies. Additionally, Kai has a keen interest in the broader societal and environmental impacts of trade and climate change policy.

name: Simeng Li
summary: Simeng started as a PhD candidate at Leiden University for the NKS (Nationaal Kennisprogramma Stikstof) project, in collaboration with TNO. Simeng studied at Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology (NUIST), where she spent seven years completing her bachelor's and master's degrees in atmospheric physics at the School of Atmospheric Physics. Her research focused on ozone depletion events and heterogeneous bromine chemistry. During this time, she received the National Scholarship, the Pacemaker to Merit Student award, and the Outstanding Graduate distinction. In January 2023, she moved to the Netherlands to begin her PhD at the Institute of Environmental Sciences (CML), Leiden University, in collaboration with TNO, under the supervision of Prof. dr. ing. Jan Willem Erisman and Dr. Enrico Dammers. Her work focuses on nitrogen modelling and emission inversion, with a particular emphasis on using observations to improve estimates of atmospheric ammonia emissions. Simeng's PhD is part of the NKS project. She is investigating atmospheric ammonia emissions and using both in situ and satellite measurements to improve emission estimates for the Netherlands.

name: Justin Lian
summary: Justin has an Engineering background in both Environmental and Mechanical Engineering. He used to work in the industry for two years. Now he aims to investigate how life cycle assessment can advance emerging technologies in the engineering field toward sustainable development. He started working as a postdoc at the Industrial Ecology department of CML in June 2022. Justin is currently a postdoctoral researcher in Industrial Ecology at CML. He received his bachelor’s degree (Environmental Engineering) and Ph.D. (Environmental Engineering) degree from The University of Nottingham and his M.Sc. (Environmental Systems Engineering) degree from University College London in the United Kingdom. His research interests are life cycle assessment for industry and engineering applications, industrial waste/pollution treatment, application of artificial intelligence algorithms to engineering, sustainability and clean energy, carbon capture and storage (CCS), microfluidics technologies including manufacturing of microdevices/chips, etc. He participated in the LEAP (Local Energy ADvanture Partnership) Micro AD project while pursuing his M.Sc. at University College London. This project demonstrated urban closed loop cycles where food waste was collected locally and anaerobically digested into renewable gas and fertilizer. Justin applied his professional skills to practice and produced a report on life cycle assessment by using SimaPro to examine the environmental impacts of the project. The report provided options and suggestions to enhance efficiency and product quality while reducing the environmental impact of the plant. Prior to joining CML, he worked in the industry for two years where he accumulated valuable working and management experiences in the industry before his next move. Justin is currently working on PROGENY (Proto-Opto-Electro-Mechanical Hybrid Systems For Generation Next Bionic Devices) project which is funded by The European Union. PROGENY has excellent academic partners from eight institutes including Leiden University, in six different European countries. Dr. Justin Lian is responsible for supporting the ongoing early-stage sustainability assessment of this new generation of technologies using life cycle assessment, working hand-in-hand with top material and technology developers in Europe.

name: Yanan Liang
summary: Yanan Liang is a postdoctoral researcher in industrial ecology whose research focuses on critical raw material stocks and flows, supply-chain resilience, and the circular economy. Her work combines IE tools like material flow analysis and scenario analysis to investigate the material requirements of the energy transition, resource dependencies, and opportunities for more sustainable and circular material systems. Yanan Liang is a postdoctoral researcher at the Institute of Environmental Sciences (CML) of Leiden University. She obtained her PhD from Leiden University in September 2024. Her doctoral thesis, The material side of the energy transition: Analyzing flows and stocks of critical and other metals, investigated the material requirements of low-carbon energy technologies, future metal demand, and the role of material stocks and recycling in the energy transition. Before joining CML as a PhD researcher in September 2019, she obtained her BSc in Civil Engineering and MSc in Industrial Engineering in China. Yanan's research interests include: She has contributed to two completed research projects at CML: Getting the Data Right, funded by the KR Foundation, focused on improving environmental data and life cycle assessment databases to support more reliable climate-footprint analysis. MaDiTraCe (Material and Digital Traceability for the Certification of Critical Raw Materials), funded by the European Union's Horizon Europe programme, explored approaches to improving the traceability, transparency, and sustainability of critical raw material supply chains through material and digital traceability technologies and certification. Her research aims to advance the sustainable and circular use of critical raw materials while strengthening supply-chain resilience.

projects.title: Material and Digital Traceability for the Certification of Critical Raw Materials (MaDiTraCe)

name: Simon van Lierde
summary: Simon started as a PhD researcher in the Industrial Ecology (IE) department of the Institute of Environmental Sciences (CML) in April 2024, focusing on enhancing data generation and sharing practices using AI and simulation tools to enhance circular manufacturing processes. Simon van Lierde earned his MSc in Industrial Ecology from Leiden University and TU Delft in 2024, where he specialized in Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA) and Geographic Information Systems (GIS). His thesis involved creating a Python-based model to predict the environmental impacts of space cooling in The Hague. Simon began his professional career at Metabolic in 2020 as a Consultant and Product Owner, developing data models in Excel and Python for circular strategies in the electronics and metals industries. His work included enhancing LCA databases, legislative research, and implementing automated sustainability reporting tools. In 2023, Simon took on the role of Data Manager at the Dutch Environmental Database, focusing on the accuracy and optimization of environmental databases for the construction industry, and fostering sustainable construction practices with industry leaders and policymakers. In April 2024, he began a PhD focusing on integrating artificial intelligence with simulation tools and traditional fieldwork to improve data collection and sharing for sustainable manufacturing.

name: Hai Lin
summary: Lin obtained his PhD from Delft University of Technology in 1993. After graduation (ir.) in Applied Mathematics at Delft University of Technology. He worked at TNO in Rijswijk from 1986 to 1990. In 1990 he joined the Department of Applied Mathematics of Delft University of Technology. Dr. Lin has many years of research experience in mathematical modelling and high performance computing. In recent years his research interests shifted to parallel numerical algorithms, modelling and simulation of large scale systems. Examples of ongoing research projects include improving the forecast of volcanic ash (cloud) transport with data assimilation, and studying the impact of wind- and solar energy to the stability of electrical power grid. Prof.dr.ir. Hai Xiang Lin will share his knowledge in mathematical modelling and high performance computing with other researchers of CML. He will actively cooperate with the Leiden Centre of Data Science (Prof.dr. Jaap van den Herik) and LIACS. Given his main appointment in Delft and having a chair now at CML will strongly support the further development of the Leiden-Delft-Erasmus Centre for Sustainability. Furthermore, he is visiting professor of the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences and Shandong University, and has been collaborating with a number of universities in China for many years.

name: Baoxiao Liu
summary: In December 2020, Baoxiao Liu joined the Institute of Environmental Sciences (CML) to pursue her doctoral degree, focusing on land-based co-benefits for carbon and biodiversity in agriculture and food system transitions. Baoxiao received her MSc (2013) in Cartography and Geographic Information System from the Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research (IGSNRR) at the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences. She previously earned a BSc (2009) in Spatial Informatics from Wuhan University in China. During her MSc, she specialized in ecological monitoring using remote sensing and GIS, focusing on land use change analysis and grassland biomass assessment. After graduation, she worked for four years as a research assistant at the National Center for Climate Change Strategy and International Cooperation (NCSC) in China, where her job involved greenhouse gas (GHG) emission inventory compilation, data management, and measuring, reporting and verification (MRV) mechanism development. Since December 2020, Baoxiao has been working at CML to pursue her doctoral degree in Industrial Ecology. Climate change and biodiversity loss are intertwined global challenges, and there is a growing recognition that joint efforts need to be pursued. Land use is the main driver of both terrestrial carbon loss and biodiversity loss. Baoxiao's current research includes understanding the spatial relationship between carbon storage and biodiversity, quantifying carbon and biodiversity loss in agriculture, and assessing the impacts of food system transitions on both carbon and biodiversity.

name: Chengyi Liu
summary: Chengyi started as a PhD researcher at the Environmental Biology department of CML in September 2022. Chengyi studied in School of Life Sciences in Sun Yat-sen University, China as an undergraduate student during 2014 - 2018, major in Life Sciences. He studied feeding ecology of Spoon-billed Sandpiper (Calidris pygmaea) in Leizhou Peninsula, China as graduation thesis and received his diploma of Bachelor degree in 2018. Later, Chengyi stuied in Evolutionary Biology Centre in Uppsala University, Sweden as a master student during 2018 – 2020, major in Ecology and Conservation. He studied how greenspace design affects attractiveness to birds and humans in urban area as graduation thesis and received his diploma of Master degree in 2020. Chengyi started his research in September 2022 in the topic of response of migratory birds to climate and land cover change.

name: Heath Logan
summary: Heath is researching the nexus between the lifetimes of consumer goods (textiles, footwear, and cosmetics), their production and end of life management, and the potential of emerging technologies in assessing the prospective environmental impacts of the design of consumer goods for safe and sustainable futures.

name: Michela Lombardi
summary: Michela Lombardi is an external PhD Candidate at Leiden University's Department of Industrial Ecology, based at ZHAW University of Applied Sciences in Switzerland. Her research focuses on spatio-temporal multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) to support informed decision-making in complex scenarios involving multiple stakeholders with divergent objectives. ​​​​​​​Michela’s academic journey began with a BSc in Global Governance at Università di Roma Tor Vergata, where environmental sustainability first emerged as a core topic in her studies. Driven by the need to model and understand complex systems through quantitative methods, she subsequently expanded her analytical capabilities by earning an MSc in Data Science from Sapienza University. Her master’s thesis further solidified her technical foundation, focusing on machine learning and the analysis of time-series GNSS satellite data to detect ionospheric disturbances linked to natural hazards. Concurrently with her university education, her expertise in Geographic Information Systems (GIS) was built in the private consulting sector. In this role, she developed applications and tackled diverse spatial challenges encompassing broad-scale spatial planning, multi-domain monitoring, risk management, and natural hazard scenario simulations. This hands-on experience sparked her drive to bridge data-driven spatial analysis with real-world decision support. The blend of policy awareness, advanced data science, and applied spatial problem-solving naturally laid the groundwork for her PhD research in spatial decision analysis. Her current research is centered on developing digital decision-support tools tailored for complex sustainability transitions. Keeping a broad perspective, she explores how spatio-temporal MCDA can be applied across critical domains such as urban planning, forest management, disaster risk reduction, and the energy transition. Her ultimate goal is to build tools that empower decision-makers of all backgrounds to navigate trade-offs and make informed choices. Beyond the technical dimensions of her work, Michela is deeply passionate about climate justice. She views the development of spatial platforms and complex systems not merely as a computational challenge, but as a powerful medium to generate a positive impact on the community.

name: Bartolomeus Häussling Löwgren
summary: Bartolomeus does his PhD on the intersection of process system engineering and industrial ecology for sustainable process and product design. At the end of Bartolomeus’ bachelor's in chemical engineering at the Technical University of Berlin, he worked one year in the chemical industry for BASF in Ludwigshafen (2018-2019) as a process analyst and finished his bachelor’s degree in 2020 with his thesis on probability modeling for data-driven surrogate models. From 2018 to 2019 Bartolomeus worked together with Odilio Alves-Filho at NTNU in Trondheim on numerical simulations and coupled heat and mass transport processes for drying processes, where he presented his research at PRES 2018 and NBDC 2019 conferences. From 2019 to 2020 Bartolomeus worked for the Process Dynamics and Operations group at the Technical University of Berlin on process modeling and optimization where he published his work on uncertainty analysis for data-driven chance-constrained optimization. During his Master’s in chemical engineering at the Technical University of Berlin (2020-2022) Bartolomeus worked for DexLeChem (2021) a green chemistry Start-Up in Berlin as a data scientist, and subsequently for CarbonMinds (2021-2022) a life-cycle inventory database provider for the chemical industry. During Bartolomeus's master's he did a project in collaboration with the Paul-Scherrer Institut on developing an open-source framework to facilitate life-cycle optimization for optimal process design problems, which he presented at the Brightcon conference (2021). He concluded his master's with the thesis “Multi-Objective Life-Cycle Optimization under Uncertainty of the German Chemical Industry” using the state-of-the-art database of the German chemical industry provided by CarbonMinds. Bartolomeus works on a joint research project with VITO on the development of a holistic sustainable process-system-design methodology and framework with applications in the chemical industry. For the methodology and framework, mathematical programming and different sustainability approaches are to be used as well as considering the uncertainty and interconnections of such systems. The aim is to quantify the environmental, societal, and economic impact of new products and processes for their complete life cycle.

name: Yuanyuan Mao
summary: Yuanyuan Mao started as a PhD researcher at the Institute of Environmental Sciences (CML) in September 2022, working on urban nature and human health. Yuanyuan Mao is PhD Candidate of Environmental Biology at the Institute of Environmental Sciences (CML) at Leiden University. She did her Master of Human Geography from the College of Geography Science at South China Normal University in 2022. During the master study, Yuanyuan specialized in ecosystem services and urbanization. Specifically, she explored the spatial-temporal evolution of urbanization and ecological environment, aiming to simulate the trend of the coupling relationship between two under 5 different scenarios with SD (System Dynamics) Model. Yuanyuan’s research revolves around the urban nature and the functions and benefits it provides to people. Her PhD research project aims to study the relationship between urban nature and human health, especially mental health. And she has a keen interest in developing and applying spatial models and tools about the ecosystem services and urban health.

name: Marc van der Meide
summary: Scientist and engineer working on the future of Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), focused on making LCA understandable and accessible. Marc holds a Cum Laude MSc degree in Industrial Ecology from Leiden University and has been working on the open source Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) tools 'Brightway2' and 'Activity Browser' since early 2018. Marc now uses his skills in creating methods and tools to provide deeper insight into -prospective- LCA models and results, both in academic work, but also useable for other LCA practitioners through his work on the 'Brightway2' and 'Activity Browser' LCA softwares.

name: Stefano Merciai
summary: Stefano started as a researcher at the Industrial Ecology department of CML in August 2019. Stefano graduated at University of Rome “La Sapienza” at the Faculty of Statistics and Economics in 2004. He started working at ISMEA, a research institute of the Italian Ministry of Agriculture, where his main task was the implementation and development of a computable general equilibrium model for the economic impact assessment of agricultural policies. During the years at ISMEA he also developed several tools for the analysis of the supply chain of agricultural products. The collaboration with ISMEA has teminated in 2016. In 2006 he started his PhD always at the University of Rome. His research aimed to develop a physical input-output model for a quantitative analysis of economic systems. During his PhD he visited for 9 months the CML-University of Leiden where he was introduced to LCA techniques. Influenced by the studies at CML, he developed a multi-dimensional input-output model where physical and economic principles coexisted in an unique tool. In 2010 he defended his thesis and soon after started working for 2.-0LCA consultants in Aalborg Denmark. There he had the opportunity to work for the construction of Exiobase, a multi-regional input-output database, within the EU-funded projects CREEA and DESIRE. His main task has been that of writing the algorithm which generated the hybrid tables of Exiobase v2 and v3. At the same time has been involved in several projects for the calculation of the carbon footprint of products and regions, the indirect land use change and LCAs. Stefano aims to develop multi-disciplinary tools for an organic and comprehensive analysis of production and consumption processes. His research focuses on developing multi-layer supply and use tables and on techniques for reconciling different data sources.

name: José Mogollón
summary: José has worked over 11 years on quantifying and modeling Earth system processes and their responses to human pressures As a researcher with a doctorate in geochemistry, he has worked for over 11 years on quantifying and modeling Earth system processes and their responses to human pressures. He obtained his Ph.D. at Utrecht University and afterward worked as a researcher at the Alfred Wegener Institute Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research, and at the NIOZ Royal Netherlands Institute for Sea Research. He has worked in several FP7 and H2020 projects and furthermore received a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Individual Fellowship to research Coastal Hypoxia at Utrecht University in conjunction with the PBL Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency. His interests are quite broad, but generally pertain to quantifying the influence and the pressures that society inflicts on the environment. This involves understanding the global biogeochemical cycles of carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus and how the Anthropocene has affected the flows and stocks of these elements through various ecosystems and reservoirs. For this he uses a range of techniques, including statistical, process-based, and mass/flow-balance models.

name: Alice Mondello
summary: Alice joined CML as a Postdoctoral researcher in the Industrial Ecology department in November 2025. She works in the Lasers4MaaS project, and her research focuses on Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) and the circular economy. Alice received her PhD in Economics, Management, and Statistics from the University of Messina in March 2025. Her doctoral research adopted a life cycle thinking perspective to support cosmetic companies in their transition towards sustainability and circularity, with a particular focus on the application of Life Cycle Assessment (LCA). After completing her PhD, Alice worked as a Postdoctoral researcher at the University of Messina, applying LCA to waste management systems. During this period, she spent six months at CML as a visiting Postdoc under the supervision of Prof. Jeroen Guinée, where she further strengthened her expertise in LCA. Alice works in the Lasers4MaaS project, which aims to develop data exchange protocols and decision-support tools for sustainable and circular manufacturing. Within the project, she is responsible for data collection and LCA analyses to support the integration of environmental information into digital twins and Digital Product Passports. Beyond the project, her research focuses on advancing the methodological development and application of LCA, with a particular interest in prospective and ex-ante approaches.

name: Athanasios Moraitis
summary: Thanasis (they/them) is an urban ecologist working on biodiversity and ecology of Urban Megaregions, specialising on insects and pollinators. Their interests revolve around contemporary urbanisations patterns and how they affect biodiversity composition. Thanasis received their Diploma on Biology (BSc), from the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki (AUTh), Greece, in 2019. They received their MSc Diploma on Conservation and Biological Resources Management with orientation Ecology and Conservation Management (AUTh, Greece), with a score of 9.84/10. In the same year they received a Certificate for the completion of professional development training for students: "Future environmentalists” (a project under the Erasmus+ programme). They have done two internships, one in 2018 at WWF Hellas offices (Athens, Greece) and another at the Forest Research Institute / Hellenic Agricultural Organization DEMETER (Thessaloniki, Greece). They have worked as a research associate at CERTH/CPERI, Greece, on EU funded projects, for three years. They are experienced in fieldwork experiments and data collection, specialising on insects and other terrestrial arthropods. More expertise revolves around ecological theory, focusing on community structure, metacommunity dynamics, responses to urbanisation and landscape dynamics. Thanasis' research is focused on untangling biodiversity patterns in urban megaregions. They are particularly interested in these contemporary urban landscapes and they way human influence changes the game of community composition for many organisms. After a year of fieldwork for data collection in the Randstad area, where they recorded Butterfly, Hoverfly and Damselfly/Dragonfly communities, they are working on the spatial, temporal and ecological patterns these communities present and how they differ among single-cities and urban megaregions.

name: Joeri Morpurgo
summary: Joeri started as a PhD researcher at the MultiGreen project in February 2021. Joeri received his MSc degree at the University of Amsterdam in 2020. During that program, Joeri followed the research major writing three MSc thesis. The first project studied the attributes of facade gardens and their relation to herbivore insects in Amsterdam and The Hague. Followed by a literature thesis on the trait distribution over the rural-urban gradient. His final project is on the relationship between elections and tropical deforestation across the pan-tropics. Infrastructure in the urban environment. Here he asses the opportunities Green infrastructure presents in regards to biodiversity and human health.

projects.title: COMBINED - increasing biodiversity and climate change resilience in Dutch landscapes

name: Juan Munizaga-Plaza
summary: Juan Antonio began as a Postdoctoral researcher in the Industrial Ecology Department at CML in September 2025. Juan Antonio is a postdoctoral researcher on the European FutuRaM (Future Availability of Secondary Raw Materials) project at the Institute of Environmental Sciences (CML) at Leiden University in the Netherlands. The FutuRaM project, funded by Horizon Europe, focuses on analysing the availability and recoverability of secondary raw materials — especially critical ones — in the EU up to 2050. Previously, Juan Antonio completed a postdoctoral position on the same FutuRaM project at the University of Munich (LMU) in Germany, where he applied material flow analysis methodologies and the United Nations Framework Classification (UNFC) to evaluate the different routes for the use and disposal of sewage sludge, as well as the recovery of phosphorus from its ashes at the regional (Bavaria), national (Germany) and European (EU) levels. He holds a degree in civil engineering from the Universidad Católica del Norte (Chile) and a master's and PhD in environmental engineering from the University of Cantabria (Spain). He has over 9 years of professional experience in university teaching, research, and development of technological and social projects focused on sustainability, the circular economy, and smart waste management. As an assistant professor at the UCN, he taught courses related to unit operations, waste management, environmental engineering and entrepreneurship. He has supervised theses and applied research projects, and actively participated in the training of students and professionals committed to environmental causes. He was the principal investigator responsible for project IT20I0084 (FONDEF, ANID - Government of Chile), which developed a technological platform to optimise waste management in public hospitals in Chile, integrating innovation, public health and sustainability. This initiative involved a team of researchers from three universities and two pilot hospitals. In the field of entrepreneurship, he founded Garbometer, a start-up that proposes digital solutions to optimise waste management in hospitals. He is also the founder of Community Lab, a citizen science and social innovation initiative that promotes sustainable neighbourhoods and ecological restoration. He has participated in entrepreneurship education and innovation incubation programmes at LMU, Babson College (USA), Luksic Scholars, Wadhwani Foundation and CISE (Spain). His work combines strategic thinking, systemic vision and a collaborative approach to address complex environmental challenges, contributing to the development of sustainable solutions with local and global impact. His research has focused on the evaluation and optimisation of waste management systems, with a particular emphasis on waste characterisation, waste prevention and minimisation, and the recovery and recycling of materials. Currently, in his research, he is interested in investigating the amount of phosphorus available in sewage sludge utilisation and disposal routes in the EU, Germany, and Bavaria; the consequences of current regulations regarding phosphorus recovery; and how the UNFC methodology proposed can help stakeholders improve their decision-making. He is also studying the LCA application to the phosphorus recovery from sewage sludge ashes.

name: Amelie Müller
summary: Amelie joined CML as a PhD candidate at the end of 2022 at the department of Industrial Ecology. Her research focuses on the refinement of Life Cycle Assessment methodology for the forest sector. Amelie obtained a Bachelor’s degree in Liberal Arts and Sciences (Major Environmental Sciences) from the Albert-Ludwigs-University in Freiburg, Germany, in 2020. Her bachelor thesis at the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems investigated the environmental impacts of PV modules with different designs and production locations. In 2022, Amelie graduated from the joint Master’s program Industrial Ecology from Leiden University and TU Delft. During her Master’s, she specialized in quantitative environmental assessment tools, such as Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), Environmental Input-Output Analysis (EIOA) and Material Flow Analysis (MFA). She conducted her master thesis in collaboration with the Institute for Networked Energy Systems of the German Aerospace Center (DLR) and investigated decarbonization pathways for the global cement industry using prospective Life Cycle Assessment. In late 2022, Amelie started a PhD at the Department of Industrial Ecology of CML in cooperation with the Flemish Institute for Technological Research (VITO) in Belgium. Amelie’s PhD research focuses on the Life Cycle Assessment methodology for forest-based products. She will improve the integration of biogenic carbon uptake in LCA methodology and open-source LCA software. Furthermore, she will investigate future production scenarios for the European forest sector using prospective LCA. Her PhD is part of the Horizon Europe project ForestPaths.

name: Timothy Na
summary: Timothy started as a PhD researcher at the Industrial Ecology department of CML in September 2024, and is focusing on infrastructure dynamics and sustainability. Timothy received his BEng degree in Chemical Engineering in 2022 at the University of Manchester. In 2024, he graduated from the MSc Industrial Ecology program at Leiden University and TU Delft. He wrote his thesis on the valuation of renewable energy resources as economic assets. His thesis was conducted simultaneously with an internship at the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), where his research on renewable energy assets contributed to the Natural Capital Compilation Guide for the 2025 System of National Accounts. Timothy’s research aims to unravel the dynamics and sustainability of infrastructure. His research will link infrastructure production, asset stock, service needs and investments to model future infrastructure dynamics and help guide infrastructure development and policymaking. His research involves using input-output analysis, and econometrics to understand infrastructure supply chains and investment as well as using material-flow analysis and life-cycle assessment to determine infrastructure’s environmental impacts.

name: Matana NG'Weli
summary: "Fostered human-carnivore coexistence: a future where humans and carnivores thrive together" Matana Levi Ng’weli is a Tanzanian wildlife research scientist and M&E expert in results-based management. He holds a BSc in Wildlife Science and Conservation from the University of Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, a Masters in Life Sciences in Biodiversity Conservation and Ecosystem Management from the Nelson Mandela African Institution of Science and Technology, Tanzania, and a Masters of Arts in Monitoring and Evaluation from the Open University of Tanzania. Matana has extensive experience in wildlife research and conservation, having served as a biodiversity scientist for both governmental and non-governmental conservation organizations in Tanzania. He has worked as a research assistant on various projects focused on birds and large mammals. His master's study, examined giraffe foraging ecology in the Tarangire-Manyara Ecosystem. This research unveiled how human influences intricately shape wildlife behaviour, emphasizing the vital need to explore animal resource selection behaviours in altered landscapes. In 2020, Matana joined the Swiss NGO (ADAP) as a Livelihoods and Natural Resources Officer before he became a Wildlife Research Scientist at the Tanzania Wildlife Research Institute (TAWIRI: in 2023), where he also leads the Serengeti lion project team in Mara, Tanzania. Matana has been at the forefront of wildlife population monitoring efforts across Tanzania, employing camera trap techniques. His expertise extends to designing and implementing effective M&E systems for results-based project/program management. Matana's research interests include wildlife population ecology, movement ecology, foraging ecology, prey-predator interactions, and the complexities of human-carnivore conflict and coexistence. His proficiency in socio-economic and ecological surveys, coupled with his analytical and problem-solving skills, underscores his commitment to achieving high-quality research outcomes. Matana’s PhD research focuses on understanding the adaptive predatory behaviors of lions and their interactions with humans in Africa’s human-wildlife interfaces, specifically within the iconic Serengeti Ecosystem in Tanzania. His research seeks to quantify and predict human-lion conflict incidents, understand changes in lion resource selection behaviors at the edges of core protected areas influenced by both environmental and anthropogenic factors, and evaluate the effectiveness of existing conflict mitigation tactics. The ultimate goal is to develop a comprehensive and effective conflict mitigation strategy that enhances community livelihoods, alleviates poverty, and preserves Africa's iconic lions.

name: Sander van Nielen
summary: Sander is a postdoctoral researcher in Industrial Ecology, with an expertise in life cycle assessment of manufactured products. Sander van Nielen has been a postdoc at CML since 2025. His areas of expertise include life cycle assessment (LCA) and Digital Product Passports. Sander obtained a BSc degree in Chemistry and an MSc in Industrial Ecology. Both are joint degrees from Leiden University and TU Delft. Afterwards, he worked for two years as a sustainability policy maker at the Municipality of Rotterdam. He completed his PhD research at the Industrial Ecology department of CML in 2024. The dissertation is titled “Environmental sustainability of NdFeB magnet recycling: foresight study on recycling systems and technologies”. As a postdoc, he contributed to the Getting the Data Right project, coordinated by Aalborg University. In this role, he created data pipelines for the collection and cleaning of monetary supply and use tables. : Sander is participating in the Lasers4MaaS project, in which he is developing methods for the automated calculation of sustainability metrics in manufacturing. These methods will be applied to create Digital Product Passports for laser-welded products.

name: Ester Oloije
summary: Ecologist studying biodiversity and sustainable rangeland management in African ecosystems. Ester is an ecologist with over 7 years of experience in wildlife research projects in Tanzania. She holds a Bachelor's degree in Wildlife Management from the College of African Wildlife Management, Mweka, and an MSc in Conservation Management of African Ecosystems from the University of Glasgow. Her work has primarily focused on wildlife ecology, disease ecology, and community-based natural resource management. She is currently a PhD candidate at Leiden University, contributing to the Curve Bend Project. Ester's PhD research focuses on biodiversity responses to collective actions in rangeland management, examining how collaborative land-use practices influence ecological outcomes in rangeland ecosystems.

name: Alexander van Oudenhoven
summary: Alexander van Oudenhoven is an environmental scientist who works on the interface between ecosystems and people. He is Education Director of the Governance of Sustainability master’s programme. Alexander specializes in quantifying and conceptualizing contributions that nature provides to humans, in relation to environmental management, spatial planning and decision making. For example, how do traditional ‘hard’ coastal protection structures (e.g. concrete dykes and barriers) compare to more nature-friendly management measures (e.g. beach nourishments), in terms of coastal protection, dune development and fishery enhancement. And how can we incorporate biodiversity and ecosystems in urban planning, so that the intensive rainfall can be captured and heat stress reduced? Alexander joined CML in May 2015 as a postdoctoral researcher as part of the NWO-TTW-funded NatureCoast project. In September 2018, he became Assistant Professor at the same institute. The main focus of Alexander’s education lies in the MSc programme Governance of Sustainability. He is acting Director of Education of the programme, supervises thesis students and coordinates the course ‘Governance of Biodiversity and Ecosystems’. Alexander also teaches at Leiden University College in the Hague, and gives guest lectures at the MSc Biology program and Minor Sustainable Development at Leiden University. Next to his work at Leiden University, Alexander was Lead Author at the ‘Intergovernmental science-policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services’ (IPBES), between 2015 and 2018. Open to all United Nations member countries, IPBES has become the leading intergovernmental body for assessing the state of the planet's biodiversity, its ecosystems and the essential services they provide to society. Alexander was responsible for the Regional Assessment for Europe and Central Asia, and is Leiden University’s IPBES focal point to the Ministry of Agriculture, Nature and Fisheries. In addition, Alexander is Co-Editor-in-Chief of Ecosystems and People, an interdisciplinary open access journal that addresses how biodiversity and ecosystems underpin human quality of life, and how societal activities and preferences drive changes in ecosystems. Alexander graduated from Wageningen University in 2008, where he obtained both his BSc and his MSc degree in the interdisciplinary field of Environmental Systems Analysis. He did an internship at the World Resources Institute (Washington, D.C.), and wrote an MSc thesis on the impacts of climate change on the spatial distribution of the oak processionary caterpillar (Thaumetopoea processionea), which constitutes a major health problem in western Europe. This work was done in collaboration with De Natuurkalender (‘Nature’s Calendar’), for which Alexander continued to work on spatial assessments of ticks (Lyme disease) and predicting pollen development (hay fever, the pollen planner). Between 2009 and early 2015, Alexander was a PhD researcher at Wageningen University, combining his PhD research with several other applied projects. His research aim was to quantify the effects of management on ecosystem services (thesis). Alexander developed a framework for indicator selection and applied and tested this framework during case studies in National Landscape ‘Het Groene Woud’ (The Netherlands), mangrove systems in Java (Indonesia) and semi-arid rangelands, both globally and in the Eastern Cape (Southern Africa). Next to his PhD, he also took part in several projects with the Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency (PBL), developing a database of ecosystem services in relation to biodiversity, land use, land cover and management. Finally, Alexander also participated in a trans-disciplinary project in Indonesia called ‘Mangrove Capital’, together with colleagues from Deltares, Wetlands International, The Nature Conservancy, Indonesian universities and several other partners. Between 2015 and 2018, Alexander was active as a post-doctoral researcher in NatureCoast, a transdisciplinary project focusing on the ‘Sand Motor’, a so-called mega-nourishment; around 21 million m3 of sand were deposited along the Ter Heijde coast, which should be sufficient for the next twenty to thirty years. One of Alexander’s tasks was the integration of NatureCoast’s research data of 12 PhD reserachers into policy-relevant information. In his current research and education, van Oudenhoven aims to embed the various concepts about human-nature relationships in policy and practice, such as ecosystem services, nature-based solutions, ecological engineering, sustainable land management. Following an transdisciplinary approach, Alexander works with municipalities, provincial authorities, water boards and (inter)national decision-makers to solve real-world problems through nature-inclusive approaches. Think of using urban green (and blue) to reduce local temperatures, increase water buffering and improve leisure opportunities, or restoring rivers to prevent flooding, improve water quality and create a more beautiful and appreciated landscape. A key aspect of Alexander’s research is the development and analysis of indicators that are both scientifically valid and feasible, but also relevant to and perceived as legitimately developed by decision makers, managers and other stakeholders.

name: Jesse Ouwehand
summary: Jesse started as a PhD researcher at the Environmental Biology department of CML in April 2023. He studies the role of the microbiome within nanotoxicity. His PhD falls under the scope of the ERC EcoWizard project (Innovative nanomaterials require ecologically-based safety assessment). He focuses on how microbes can alter the response to nanomaterials. With the aim to generalise and unravel the role of the microbiome within nanosafety. Jesse started his studies at the Hogeschool Leiden with the BSc Biomedical Research and graduated on a project on the antibacterial activity of plant-derived compounds on S. aureus biofilms. He continued his studies at Leiden University with the MSc Biology From Cells to Organisms specialising in evolutionary, cell biology and bioinformatics. During his master, he studied the species distribution of Triturus newts in the Balkan Peninsula and graduated on a project on the effect of carbon sources on the morphology of Streptomyces.

name: Aaron Paris
summary: Aaron is a PhD student in Industrial Ecology working on the prospective sustainability assessment of large-scale economic systems. In 2024, Aaron completed his MSc in Industrial Ecology at Leiden University and Delft University of Technology. In his master's thesis, he examined the inequality of environmental footprints across income groups in the EU. Before this, he worked as a researcher at the University of Kassel, focusing on decarbonization strategies for companies. He also holds an MSc and a BSc in Industrial Engineering from the universities of Kassel and Rostock, Germany. Aaron works on coupling prospective Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) with dynamic Material Flow Analysis (MFA) and System Dynamics to assess the future environmental sustainability of large-scale economic systems. His research aims to create prospective spatiotemporal life cycle inventories and evaluate mitigation scenarios against global sustainability targets. For any questions, you are most welcome to contact him.

name: Nils Pauliks
summary: Nils joined the Industrial Ecology department of CML in January 2024 as a PhD researcher and is working on the on circular electronics in the Circular Circuits project using Material Flow Analysis (MFA) and Life Cycle Assessment (LCA). Nils earned his bachelor’s degree in environmental engineering from RWTH Aachen University in Germany in 2021. Concurrently, he served as a student researcher at the Institute of Sustainability in Civil Engineering (INaB), engaging in research projects centered around life cycle assessment (LCA) for sustainable steelmaking and the life cycle sustainability assessment of renewable energy. In 2023, he successfully completed the joint master's program in Industrial Ecology at Leiden University and TU Delft. His master's thesis explored applications of machine learning in ex-LCA, making a substantial contribution to mitigating uncertainty in this field. The research project, Circular Circuits, aims to improve the environmental sustainability of electronic products by assessing circular strategies such as recycling, remanufacture, or reuse. The first part of the research is targeted to quantify the electrical and electronic equipment in the Dutch economy. Material Flow Analysis is used to conduct scenarios of potential future development as well as to assess the effectiveness of circular strategies. The second part will use Life Cycle Assessment to identify hotspots of environmental impacts, starting from the extraction of resources to the end-of-life phase, and define potential solutions for the industry. For any questions, you are most welcome to contact him.

projects.title: Circular Circuits

name: Adrien Perello-y-Bestard
summary: Adrien is a PhD candidate in Industrial Ecology, working on novel computational methods for sustainability impact assessments and decision-making. Adrien earned his first master’s degree in cognitive engineering in 2010. His journey since then has been shaped by a diverse range of experiences, including working in the nuclear industry, volunteering in eco-communities, and a two-year cycling expedition around the world. These experiences deepened his understanding of the environmental impacts of the Anthropocene. Motivated by his passion for sustainability and a desire to pursue an academic career, Adrien returned to study Industrial Ecology at Leiden University, where he graduated in 2024. During his studies, he worked as a research assistant on the Futuram project, focusing on extending material flow analysis models to track hierarchical composition layers. His master’s thesis investigated the recoverability of critical raw materials from European electric vehicles in the context of the 2023 EU Battery Directive. Adrien's research focuses on advancing computational methods to support the Safe and Sustainable by Design (SSbD) framework as part of the EU-funded INSIGHT project. His work focuses on two key areas: first, integrating life cycle impact assessment models with a comprehensive knowledge graph that connects diverse datasets on health, environmental, social, and economic factors; and second, developing decision support tools to navigate trade-offs and uncertainties, particularly for high-throughput screening of advanced chemicals and materials.

name: Mariana Braz Pires
summary: Mariana is a PhD researcher at CML, focusing on building large-scale predictive models to assess the impact of current and future mining activities on freshwater ecosystems and developing biodiversity-inclusive strategies for the energy transition. Mariana completed her BSc degree in Mathematics at University of Aveiro (Portugal) in 2020. Subsequently, she pivoted her academic trajectory towards Environmental Science, having obtained a MSc degree in this field at Utrecht University (The Netherlands), where she followed a track focused on Environmental Change and Ecosystems. During her Master’s degree, Mariana was able to apply her knowledge and skills in Theoretical Mathematics, Statistics and Programming to ecological and environmental research, by employing different mathematical modelling and analysis techniques. In her Master’s thesis, conducted in collaboration with the University of Patras (Greece), Mariana assessed the potential synergistic impact of climate and land-use change on the entire endemic flora of a regional endemism centre in Greece, and identified plant biodiversity conservation gaps and priorities. Mariana’s research focuses on developing biodiversity-inclusive strategies for the energy transition, specifically addressing the impact of mining activities on freshwater ecosystems. She will develop large-scale models (continental to global) to predict the effects of current and future mining activities on freshwater resources and biodiversity, which will involve interdisciplinary work at the intersection of ecology and hydrology. These models will not only be employed to carry out global impact assessments but also to enhance the characterization of mining impacts on biodiversity within sustainability assessment tools.

name: Sophie Planchenault
summary: Sophie started as a PhD Candidate at the Environmental Biology department of CML in January 2023. Sophie received her BSc in Natural Sciences in 2020 from Université Claude Bernard (Lyon, France) and her MSc in Ecology and Evolution in 2022 from Université Paul Sabatier (Toulouse, France).She conducted her Master's thesis at the Laboratory of Functional Ecology and Environmental Sciences (LEFE, Toulouse, France), where she focused on the role of photosynthetic microorganisms in peatland carbon dynamics. More specifically, how their presence, secondary metabolites (exudates) and necromass affect soil microbial communities, trophic interactions within the soil food web and biogeochemical processes. In January 2023, Sophie moved to the Netherlands to join the Environmental Biology department of CML to start her PhD on the role of microbial diversity in soil carbon dynamics. Sophie's PhD research project aims to unravel the role of microbial diversity in soil organic matter formation and stabilization, and therefore its outcome on carbon dynamics. She wants to put an emphasis on studying the intricate link between microbial community composition, food web interactions and carbon cycling.

name: Martin van der Plas
summary: Martin is the team lead of the Field and Lab Support team. Together with the technicians, he works to ensure that lab and fieldwork are carried out safely and efficiently. He has a background in molecular biology and ecotoxicology, with experience in a wide range of techniques used at CML, both in the lab and in the field. Martin obtained his BSc (2016) and MSc (2019) from Leiden University. During his bachelor’s, he focused on ecology and related disciplines, before shifting to the molecular side of biology in his master’s, where he specialized in molecular genetics and biotechnology. As part of his MSc, he completed two research internships. The first investigated the prevalence of psittacine beak and feather disease in ring-necked parakeets in the Netherlands using scat sample barcoding. The second focused on myelin development in early vertebrates, combining nerve tissue staining with RNA transcriptomics across developmental stages. After graduating, Martin worked as a research assistant at Naturalis Biodiversity Center on sponge barcoding, and at the Institute of Environmental Sciences (CML) on monitoring the invasive Dreissena bugensis in the Rijnland area using eDNA. From 2021 to 2026, Martin pursued a PhD at CML within the ecotoxicology group. His research focuses on the application of eDNA in ecotoxicology, both as a tool to assess community-level effects of stressors such as nanoparticles, and as a predictive method for evaluating ecosystem health. From January 2026 Martin has been the team lead of the Field and Lab Support team.

name: Merle Praum
summary: Merle started as a collaborative PhD candidate at both the CML and the European Commission Joint Research Centre (JRC) in Sevilla in October 2026, aiding in the ACT! consortium project. Her research focuses on modelling the impacts of Circular Economy measures and aims to bridge the gap between bottom-up and top-down modelling approaches. Merle obtained a Bachelor's in Econometrics and Operations Research at Maastricht University and continued with a MPhil and MSc in Business Data Science at the Tinbergen Institute, jointly hosted by Erasmus University Rotterdam, Universiteit van Amsterdam and Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. She spent a semester abroad at the National University of Singapore. Her BSc Thesis on Game Theory modelling won the Natalies Best Bachelor Thesis prize. Her master thesis was in collaboration with the Amsterdam Medical Center (AMC) and employed Deep Learning for medication response predictions. During her Master’s, her main interests were modeling, simulation, optimization, and prediction. Before starting her PhD studies, Merle worked as a scientific trainee at the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre in Seville. In this role, she analyzed the competitiveness potential of various circular economy technologies for the EU using Economic Complexity frameworks. In October 2026, Merle started a PhD at the CML and the European Commission Joint Research Centre (JRC) Sevilla, Unit of Circular Economy. Material and resource use in present-day society is largely linear and extractive, systemically linked to climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution, and resource scarcity. An accelerated transition to a circular economy (CE) is needed to address these challenges. Merle's doctoral project develops methods to link bottom-up and top-down approaches into an integrated micro–macro modelling suite for circular economy policy support. This includes building detailed bottom-up stock and flow data; mapping regional and sectoral shifts in asset ownership, value-capture and diffusion potential of circular solutions; connecting these bottom-up datasets to dynamic top-down CGE models bidirectionally.

name: Peiyan Qin
summary: Peiyan started as a PhD researcher at the Department of Environmental Biology of CML in September 2024. He investigates the impacts of nano- and microplatics on plant-soil-microbe interactions in terrestrial agroecosystems. Peiyan Qin graduated with a Bachelor of Science degree in Biological Sciences from Northwest A&F University in 2021. In his undergraduate thesis, he investigated the effects of conventional petroleum-based microplastics on the ecological characteristics and functions of bacterial communities in various soil ecosystems. In 2024, he obtained a Master of Science degree in Microbiology from the same university. During his master's studies, he researched the impact of microplastics under salt stress on plant growth and rhizosphere microbial communities, as well as their influence on soil priming effects and carbon turnover processes. Peiyan's research topic is on the impacts of nano- and microplatics on plant-soil-microbe interactions in terrestrial agroecosystems.

name: Danny Lopes Ramos
summary: Danny began his PhD in January 2025 in the Environmental Biology department at CML. His research focuses on soil ecology and microbiology, with the aim of linking fungal traits to ecosystem functions. He uses mesocosm experiments, manipulating either functions or fungal traits to better understand the relationship between traits and ecosystem multifunctionality. Danny holds a BSc in Earth and Environmental Sciences from the University of Rennes, with a focus on soil sciences and ecosystem ecology. He then completed an MSc in Physical Geography and Ecosystem Sciences at Lund University, specializing in soil and plant ecology, biogeochemical cycles, and ecosystem analysis. During this program, he conducted his MSc thesis on fungal biomass and decomposition, alongside additional experimental work on fungal community composition and tundra ecosystems. His work combined field and laboratory approaches with analytical methods such as spectroscopy, qPCR, isotopic tracing, and data analysis. Danny works on fungal traits and soil multifunctionality. The aim of the project is to understand how fungal trait diversity drives key ecosystem functions (carbon cycling, soil structure). Building on trait-based ecology frameworks established for plants, his research extends this approach to fungi to explore what mechanisms and patterns can be uncovered

name: Sowmya Marriyapillai Ravisandiran
summary: Sowmya joined as a PhD candidate at CML-Industrial Ecology as a part of the FutuRaM project, and is working on assessing material recovery from municipal solid waste since November 2023 In 2020, she completed her Bachelors in Engineering Physics from IIT Bombay in India. She obtained her MSc in Industrial Ecology from Leiden University and TU Delft in 2023. In her master’s thesis she studied the contribution of informal waste sector in plastic waste management in the city of Chennai, India, using a combined qualitative analysis and material flow analysis (MFA). Her PhD research is a part of the FutuRam project, which tries to assess the availability of secondary raw material in waste streams in the EU. In this, she is specifically working on the municipal solid waste (MSW) stream, to assess the quantity and potential recoverability of critical raw materials that end up in MSW incineration ashes.

name: Lavinia Reitz
summary: After completing her Master’s degree in Physics in 2022, Lavinia joined Forschungszentrum Jülich, shifting her research to Life Cycle Assessment of ship-based carbon capture. In 2024 she started her PhD with Bernhard Steubing at Leiden University, assessing prospective environmental and sustainability impacts of Direct Air Capture and Storage systems. During her Bachelor studies in Physics at the University of Bonn, Lavinia focused on particle physics, researching the potential existence of Leptoqarks and how to find them in the ATLAS experiment at CERN. Similarly, her Master’s studies were focused on experimental particle physics, but then turned to researching renewable energy generation potentials using Airborne Wind Energy technologies, in collaboration with the TU Delft. The thesis work was continued and applied in a short project work for TU Delft researching potentials for specific operation sites. Afterwards, Lavinia joined Forschungszentrum Jülich, shifting her research to Life Cycle Assessment, applied to ship-based carbon capture within the EverLoNG project. During her PhD studies, Lavinia investigates Direct Air Capture (DAC) technologies within the DACStorE project (https://www.dacstore-project.com/en) at Forschungszentrum Jülich, Institute of Climate and Energy Systems - Juelich Systems Analysis (ICE-2). She evaluates current and future impacts of DAC and storage using prospective life cycle assessment and life cycle sustainability assessment methodologies. Bernhard Steubing and Paul Behrens supervise her PhD at University Leiden, and Christina Wulf at ICE-2.

name: Roy Remme
summary: Roy Remme is an environmental scientist who works on urban nature and its importance to people, predominantly through the development and application of spatial decision-support tools. Roy is an environmental scientist who works on urban nature and its importance to people, predominantly through the development and application of spatial decision-support tools. He worked for the Natural Capital Project at Stanford University between 2018-2020, to co-develop and apply urban ecosystem service models in the InVEST (Integrated Valuation of Ecosystem Services and Tradeoffs) software suite. Between 2015-2018 Roy worked at RIVM, where he co-developed the Dutch Natural Capital Model and worked on the Atlas of Natural Capital and the TEEB-Stad tool, to assess, quantify, and value natural capital in the Netherlands. Simultaneously, he also helped develop the first ecosystem accounts for the Netherlands at CBS (Statistics Netherlands). Roy did his PhD research at Wageningen University, on spatial analysis of ecosystem services and biodiversity and the design and testing of ecosystem accounts. He studied Environmental Sciences (BSc) at Utrecht University, and Climate Studies (MSc) at Wageningen University. Roy is associate editor at the journal Ecosystem Services. Roy’s research revolves around the importance of nature in cities and the benefits it provides to people. He is interested in understanding how, when, and where nature impacts people, who benefits from nature, and how the benefits of nature can be leveraged to develop more sustainable, resilient, and healthy cities. His research straddles multiple fields, including ecology, geography, environmental economics, and environmental governance. He has a keen interest in developing and applying spatial models and tools that inform decision-making.

projects.title: COMBINED - increasing biodiversity and climate change resilience in Dutch landscapes

name: Carlos Felipe Blanco Rocha
summary: Carlos Felipe obtained his PhD degree at the Institute of Environmental Sciences (CML), where he also obtained his M.Sc. degree in Industrial Ecology. He also holds a Bachelor’s degree in Environmental Engineering from Universidad de Los Andes in Colombia. Between 2006-2014, Carlos Felipe worked in the mining industry as a Health, Safety, Environment and Community Relations (HSEC) manager in several countries in Latin America including Chile, Peru, Colombia, Guyana and Brazil. In these roles, he led social and environmental impact studies for mining and minerals exploration projects, developed environmental mine closure plans and served as a lead EHS critical incident investigator. He was also tasked with environmental auditing and implementing ISO14001 and OHSAS18001 standards and related training programmes. In the period 2014-2018 Carlos Felipe worked as an independent sustainability consultant for the mining, energy and forestry sectors and developed software solutions for stakeholder engagement programs in several large-scale mining projects. In his PhD thesis, Carlos Felipe proposed various methods to appraise the safety and sustainability of emerging technologies and demonstrated them with a case study of high-efficiency III-V/Silicon solar cells. In his MSc thesis, Carlos Felipe developed a framework to assess ecosystem services in LCA and demonstrated it by a case study of water supply for mining in the north of Chile. The M.Sc. thesis was awarded the Stans prize by CML in 2016. Carlos Felipe’s current research focus is Life Cycle Sustainability Assessment (including LCA and Social-LCA) and Ecological Risk Assessment of emerging technologies with a special focus on safe and sustainable design of energy technologies. Developing quantitative forward-looking models in these domains requires comprehensive and robust methods for scenario analysis, uncertainty analysis and global sensitivity analysis. Carlos Felipe’s current research aims to increase the applicability and usefulness of such methods in the field of sustainability and to establish linkages with developments in related fields such as Bayesian Analysis and Machine Learning. Carlos Felipe is currently a main lecturer for the course Society’s Metabolism in the Industrial Ecology master’s programme and supports the LCA Practice & Reporting course offered by the same programme. He is also the main lecturer for the course Environment & Development offered by Leiden University College.
